phonemes.desc: Short epsilon with rough breathing, pitched high — the name exhales authority.
Rho plus long alpha — the final syllable opens broadly, like a queen's gesture.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HAY-rah' — the first syllable is sharp and pitched; the final 'a' is long and open.

kin.label: Greek (disputed)
kin.form: ὥρα (hōra), 'season, time' — the older derivation of Ἥρα, making her the goddess of the ritual year (Fick, Chantraine); now widely doubted

kin.label: Mycenaean Greek
kin.form: e-ra, attested in Linear B at Pylos (PY Tn 316) — among the earliest offerings on record to the future Olympian pantheon

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ἥρως (hērōs), 'hero' — Beekes judges both words Pre-Greek and plausibly related; the lexicon gloss 'Lady, mistress' reflects this uncertain cluster

pronunciation.note: Hēra is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἥρᾱ contains both stress (acute on the initial η) and length (long final alpha).

domains.title: The Queen of Olympus
domains.subtitle: Marriage, Sovereignty, Women, and the Ritual Year
domains.lead: Hēra is the queen of the gods by marriage, and her mythology is the mythology of what that costs. She defends the legitimacy of the Olympian order — marriage, kingship, sworn oaths — with a ferocity born of defending it constantly against her own husband.

cards.name: Marriage and Fidelity
cards.desc: Patron of the wedded state; the gamos, or sacred marriage, is her rite.

cards.name: Royal Sovereignty
cards.desc: Queen of gods and men; kingship legitimized through her partnership with Zeús.

cards.name: Childbirth
cards.desc: Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth and her own daughter, acts at her command to protect women in labor.

cards.name: The Peacock
cards.desc: The hundred-eyed Argos, her faithful watcher, set into the tail of her sacred bird (Ovid, Met. 1.721–723).

symbols.name: Peacock
symbols.meaning: The transformed Argos Panoptês, whose hundred eyes still watch from its tail

symbols.name: Pomegranate
symbols.meaning: Fertility, marriage, and the sealed storehouse of the dead

symbols.name: Sceptre
symbols.meaning: Queenship and authority; she sits enthroned beside Zeús as co-ruler

symbols.name: Polos crown
symbols.meaning: The cylindrical crown of the great Near Eastern goddess-queens — Hēra's regalia, kin to Cybele's and Aštart's

symbols.name: Cow
symbols.meaning: Her sacred animal at Argos; Homer's formula 'ox-eyed Hēra' (e.g., Iliad 1.551) preserves the association

mythology.lead: Hēra's myths are almost all variations on one theme: the wronged wife defending her throne. She cannot overthrow Zeús, but she can punish his lovers and their children with relentless ingenuity — and beneath the vengeance the sources preserve traces of a far older, cosmic Hēra.

myths.title: The Cuckoo and the Daedala
myths.text: Greek tradition set the wooing of Hēra at Plataea in Boeotia. Pausanias (9.2.7–9.3.8) describes the local festival of the Daedala, at which wooden images were dressed as brides and burned on Mount Cithaeron — reenacting, the Plataeans said, the very origin of marriage: Zeús, unable to win the angry, aloof Hēra, had a wooden image dressed and carried in wedding procession; Hēra stormed up to tear the bride apart, found an oak instead — and laughed, and was reconciled. Elsewhere the wooing is told with a cuckoo: Zeús first approached her in bird form, and she cradled him in her lap (a tale preserved in the Byzantine scholia). Hēra's marriage to Zeús was the cosmos's founding contract — the hieros gamos that every Greek wedding ritually repeated — and the myths insist it began in deception before it became the pillar of order.

myths.title: The Persecution of Hēraklēs
myths.text: Hēra's most famous feud is with Hēraklēs, living proof of Zeús's adultery with the mortal Alkmene. She sent two serpents to his cradle, and the infant strangled both (Pindar, Nemean 1.33–72). Years later she drove him to the madness in which he killed his own wife and children, and it was her will, working through Eurystheus, that imposed the Twelve Labors (Euripides, Heracles; Apollodorus 2.4.12). Yet the feud is also the making of him: each labor forces the hero past mortal limits until, burned alive on Oeta, he is taken up to Olympus — where, in the Odyssey's quiet ending (11.601–604), he has for his wife Hebe of the beautiful ankles, given him by Hēra herself. The persecutor crowns her enemy. The myth turns vengeance into the engine of apotheosis: without Hēra's hatred there is no Hēraklēs.

myths.title: Argos Panoptês
myths.text: When Zeús desired the Argive princess Io, Hēra could not punish her husband — so she punished the beloved. Zeús turned Io into a cow; Hēra took the cow and set it under guard, and the guard she chose was Argos Panoptês, 'the all-seeing' — a giant with a hundred eyes that never all slept at once (Apollodorus 2.1.3; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.568–723). Zeús sent Hermês, who lulled the hundred eyes with the long, wandering tale of Syrinx's transformation, struck off the head with his sword, and freed Io. Hēra collected the hundred eyes and set them in the tail of her sacred bird, the peacock (Ovid 1.721–723), so that Argos's vigilance survives, reassigned to her own service. The queen's grief is the more terrible for being constitutional: she can never touch Zeús, so her vigilance falls outward — and the sky rains transformations.

myths.title: The Binding of Zeús
myths.text: The Iliad preserves, almost in passing, the most radical thing ever said about Hēra. Threatened with Zeús's violence over the Trojan War, she answers that she remembers when she, Poseidôn, and Athēnâ had actually bound Zeús (1.396–406) — a plot whose possibility implies a Hēra far older and more powerful than the wronged wife of epic. The story has a sequel: Thetis, summoned by the hundred-handed Briareos — whom the gods call Aigaion — came up to Olympus and sat beside Zeús, and the gods, in awe, abandoned their chains. Homer offers no theology of the episode; he needs it to explain why Thetis could sway the king of gods. But it survives as a fossil of a pre-Olympian order: before she was consort, Hēra was a cosmic sovereign, and Zeús's throne was once contested by her faction and held only with the help of the oldest power in the sea.

myths.title: The Milk of the Goddess
myths.text: A cluster of late-antique star-myths gave Hēra's milk a permanent place in the sky. Hēraklēs, hidden by Athēnâ at Hēra's breast so that suckling would make him immortal, bit too hard; the goddess flung him off, and her milk spurted across the heavens — the Milky Way (Eratosthenes, Catasterisms fr. 44; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.43). The tales are playful, but their premise is the myth's own: Hēra is the nurse of immortality itself. Every Olympian apotheosis runs through her — Hēraklēs receives her daughter Hebe as his bride; the hero's immortality is her final gift; the king's legitimacy is her dowry. Where her milk touches, mortality ends; where she withholds it, heroes remain men. Even the galaxy, in this tradition, is a trace of her body. A myth that makes the Milky Way a spill of the queen's milk is a myth about the reach of legitimacy: everything above the earth, it says, once depended on her breast.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Hēra with Iuno, the queen of the Roman gods and protector of marriage. Iuno was central to the Roman state cult; every woman had a personal Iuno, just as every man had a personal Genius. In the Hellenistic east, Hēra was syncretized with Egyptian Isis and Phoenician Astarte as a supreme queen goddess. Her great sanctuaries at Argos and Samos were among the richest in Greece, and the Heraia festival at Olympia included athletic competitions for women. The very word 'hero' is probably unrelated to her name, but the association has shaped her reception for centuries.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hēra is the archetype of the queen consort — powerful because of her position, dangerous because of her pride. Her peacock remains a symbol of beauty and watchfulness; her jealousy has been a literary theme from Euripides to opera. The Argive Heraion, her massive sanctuary near Argos, dominated the plain and testified to her political importance; Argos claimed to be her favorite city. In modern feminist readings, Hēra has been reinterpreted as a figure of constrained power, a goddess whose authority is real but always mediated through marriage. Restoring Hēra restores the name of the goddess who made marriage a cosmic institution.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Hēra is the goddess of the institution that survives passion. Her marriage to Zeús is not romantic; it is the pillar of cosmic order. Every affair threatens not just her dignity but the legitimacy of Olympus itself. That is why her vengeance is implacable: she is not merely jealous, she is defending the structure of things.

The modern world has largely abandoned the idea that marriage is cosmic. Hēra's name therefore sounds archaic, even oppressive. But her deeper insight remains: some bonds must be defended, not because they are always happy, but because their collapse undoes everything built upon them. The restoration of her name is a reminder that sovereignty has always depended on loyalty.
lore.archaeology: The Argive Heraion, on a terrace above the Argive plain, was among the greatest sanctuaries of the Greek world: votives run back to the Geometric period, and a colossal fifth-century Doric temple rose under Argive patronage, excavated by the American School from 1892. On Samos the Heraion — whose first great temple was built by the architect Rhoikos around 560 BCE — held a wooden image so old the Samians said it had fallen from the sky (Pausanias 7.4.4–5). At Olympia the Heraion (c. 590 BCE) is the earliest known Doric temple whose columns still stand, and Pausanias (5.16.2–8) records the Heraia, athletic games for maidens run in her honor every fourth year.
